The air in Elara’s bedroom grew heavy and cold, the kind of sudden, unnatural chill that sinks past the skin and into the bone. Outside, a sliver of moon hung in an inky sky, but inside, a different light began to bloom in the corner near her wardrobe. It was a faint, phosphorescent green, the color of deep-sea life, and it pulsed with a slow, hypnotic rhythm.

From this sickly glow, a creature began to coalesce. It was not born of flesh and blood, but of shadow and spectral light. It had a long, serpentine form, like an eel made of captured starlight and dread. It had no eyes, but the air itself seemed to bend around its tapered head, as if reality was being perceived and judged. It moved without sound, flowing over the wooden floor like a ribbon of viscous liquid, leaving a faint, cold trail that glittered for a moment before vanishing.

Elara slept on, tangled in her sheets, her breathing slow and even. The creature ascended the bed, its form casting no weight. It paused at the foot of the mattress, its featureless head swaying, as if tasting the scent of her life, her warmth, her dreaming mind. It was an ancient thing, a being that swam in the currents between worlds, and it had been drawn to the quiet, dormant energy of her sleeping body.

It moved up the length of the bed, a slithering tendril of otherworldly cold. As it neared the curve of her hip, Elara stirred in her sleep. Her dream, a placid meadow, began to curdle. The grass turned to cold, black water, and she felt a sense of immense pressure, of being pulled down into an abyss.

The creature’s head reached the base of her spine. It did not push or force. Instead, it phased. The tip of its form became translucent, wavering like a heat haze before sinking into her skin. There was no pain, no physical tearing, only a profound, invasive cold that shot through her nerves.

In her dream, the black water rushed into her mouth, a silent, icy drowning. She felt something long and smooth slide past her, coiling in the depths of her dream-self. Awake, her body arched instinctively. A single, sharp gasp escaped her lips, a tiny puff of condensation in the frigid air. Her eyes remained closed, but her subconscious screamed.

The creature unspooled itself, pouring its ethereal body into hers. It was a violation on a level she had no words for, a trespass against the very architecture of her being. She felt it not as a physical presence, but as a line of frost being drawn up her spine from the inside, a thread of absolute cold weaving itself into the warmth of her core. It was a feeling of being hollowed out and occupied simultaneously, a space within her that had never been a space suddenly filled by an alien geometry.

When the last inch of its luminous tail had vanished, the unholy green light in the room died. The air slowly began to warm, returning to normal.

Elara’s body relaxed, settling back into the mattress. Her dream shifted one last time. She was floating in a dark, silent space, no longer drowning, but adrift. And she could feel a faint, rhythmic pulse beside her own heartbeat. A cold, steady, and patient presence that was now part of her.

She would wake in the morning feeling strangely empty and profoundly violated, with a lingering, deep-seated chill she would never be able to shake. The room would look the same, her body would bear no mark, but she would know, with an unshakeable and terrifying certainty, that she was no longer alone in her own body.
